Fetal Echo Project · Unit F2 · Foundation tier · v0.3

Fetal rhythm: tools and mechanisms

DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

You will be able to

  • State what counts as an abnormal sustained fetal heart rate.
  • Describe how M-mode, pulsed-wave Doppler and tissue Doppler time the atria against the ventricles.
  • Tell a premature atrial beat from a premature ventricular beat.
  • Recognise the patterns of the main fast and slow rhythms.
  • Explain why blocked atrial beats must be told apart from heart block.

Every study records the rhythm

Every fetal echocardiogram must document the fetal heart rate and rhythm.1

When the rhythm is irregular, or the rate is slow or fast, the mechanism should be documented with M-mode, pulsed-wave Doppler or tissue Doppler, alone or together.2

Normal and abnormal rates

The normal fetal heart rate ranges from 120 to 160 beats per minute.3,4

The echocardiography guideline describes a sustained rate below 120 beats per minute as abnormal at any gestation. For the upper limit it gives a range: a sustained rate above 160 to 180 is abnormal.5,6

The screening guideline sets its thresholds for referral at a persistent rate of 110 or less, and 180 or more.7,8

The principle: time the atria against the ventricles

In a fetal echocardiogram the rhythm is worked out from movement and flow: when does each atrial contraction happen, when does each ventricular contraction happen, and how are the two related?

M-mode: the cursor passes through an atrial wall and the free wall of a ventricle together. Its high temporal resolution allows precise timing of atrial and ventricular contraction.9

Pulsed-wave Doppler: two flows are sampled at once so that atrial and ventricular events appear on one trace. The pairs are superior vena cava with ascending aorta, mitral inflow with aortic outflow, and pulmonary artery with pulmonary vein.10

In suspected supraventricular tachycardia the guideline advises against the mitral inflow and aortic outflow pair, because the inflow waves fuse and the atrial timing is hidden.11

Tissue Doppler at the lateral mitral or tricuspid annulus records myocardial velocities and time intervals and may help in assessing rhythm.9,10,12,11

ToolWhat is recorded together
M-modeAn atrial wall and a ventricular free wall
Pulsed-wave DopplerSuperior vena cava with ascending aorta
Pulsed-wave DopplerMitral inflow with aortic outflow (not advised in suspected supraventricular tachycardia)
Pulsed-wave DopplerPulmonary artery with pulmonary vein
Tissue DopplerMyocardial velocities and time intervals at the lateral mitral or tricuspid annulus

Premature beats

A premature atrial beat resets the atrial rhythm, so the pause that follows is incomplete.13

With a premature ventricular beat, the interval between successive atrial beats is preserved.14

Ectopic beats are the most common rhythm disturbance and are often benign. Frequent episodes, more often than every three to five beats, or a rhythm that stays irregular for more than one to two weeks, are an indication for further assessment.15,16

Fast rhythms

The patterns the guideline describes for fast rhythms.17,18,19,20,21

RhythmAtria and ventriclesDistinguishing feature
Sinus tachycardiaOne to one, regularLong interval from ventricular to atrial contraction; rate below 200 per minute
Re-entrant supraventricular tachycardia through an accessory pathway (the common form)One to oneShort interval from ventricle to atrium
Ectopic atrial tachycardia; permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardiaOne to oneLong interval from ventricle to atrium
Atrial flutterOften only every second or third atrial beat reaches the ventriclesRapid sawtooth atrial movement on M-mode
Ventricular tachycardiaAtrial contractions independent of the ventricular rhythmShown by M-mode or by paired arterial and venous Doppler

A persistent rate of 180 or more found at screening should be evaluated further for a tachyarrhythmia or fetal hypoxia.8

Slow rhythms

The patterns the guideline describes for slow rhythms.22,23,24

RhythmAtria and ventriclesDistinguishing feature
Sinus bradycardiaRecorded together with any modalityMost have a ventricular rate above 90 to 100 per minute
Blocked premature atrial beats, repeated-Can mimic second- or third-degree block and must be told apart from it
Complete heart blockIndependent of each otherVentricular rate typically 50 to 80 per minute

The screening guideline names the same three possibilities for a persistent slow rate: frequent blocked atrial ectopic beats, atrioventricular block and sinus bradycardia.7

Tissue Doppler at the lateral tricuspid annulus is named as a possible aid in sinus bradycardia.12

Maternal antibodies

When the pregnant patient carries anti-Ro or anti-La antibodies, the fetal mechanical PR interval may be measured to assess atrioventricular conduction.25

The evidence is unclear that routine surveillance of these fetuses reduces progression to higher-degree atrioventricular block.26

Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies are a listed indication for fetal echocardiography.27,28

When the rhythm is not sinus, read function with care

Outside sinus rhythm, reversal of the venous A-wave is an unreliable indicator of worsening cardiac function.29

Working out a rhythm

  • Rate and rhythm documented1
  • If abnormal: mechanism documented with M-mode, pulsed-wave Doppler or tissue Doppler2
  • Atrial and ventricular events shown on one trace9,10
  • Fast rhythm: mitral inflow and aortic outflow pair avoided for atrial timing11
  • Slow rhythm: blocked atrial beats told apart from atrioventricular block24
  • Venous A-wave reversal not relied on as a sign of worsening function when the rhythm is not sinus29
